title: Saying No: Negation
description: Three little words carry every 'no' in Gulf Arabic — ما before verbs, مو before everything else, لا for commands — plus never, nobody, nothing at all, and the art of refusing a plate of food without offending anyone.
approach: GPA Phase 2 — pattern noticing. Comedy sketches full of refusals are watched first; the three-way split is then made explicit and drilled by sorting, before the learner practises the refusal ritual aloud.
unlock_condition: ≥13/16 on the ما / مو / لا sorting quiz and a recorded polite refusal

grammar.title: ما for verbs, مو for everything else, لا for commands
grammar.explanation: Gulf Arabic splits 'not' three ways. Before a verb — any tense — use ما: ما أشرب 'I don't drink', ما رحت 'I didn't go'. The 'have' words عندي، معي، فيه count as verbs here, so it is ما عندي, ما فيه. Before a noun, an adjective or a pronoun use مو: هو مو هني 'he isn't here', السيارة مو جديدة 'the car isn't new'. Emiratis and Qataris say مب instead of مو; Najdi Saudis sometimes ماهوب — same job, pick one and stay with it. Telling someone not to do something takes لا plus the present verb: لا تروح 'don't go'. The formal ليس and the Egyptian مش are never used.

culture.title: The first no is not a no
culture.note: When a Gulf host offers food, the first refusal is part of the offer: the guest says لا، شكراً, the host insists, the guest gives in a little. Refusing once is polite; accepting immediately can look greedy; refusing three times means you actually mean it. So a real 'no' needs more than لا. Add a blessing — الله يخليك, الله يعافيك — and a reason the host cannot argue with: والله شبعت 'I swear I'm full'. The word بس 'enough' with a hand over the cup stops a coffee refill without a word spoken. Nobody loses face, and the host has done their duty.

phrases.english: Just have one bite (the host's insistence)

vocabulary.teaching_note: The word that says 'is not' without a verb: هذا مو بيتي. Kuwait, Saudi, Bahrain and Qatar say مو; the UAE says مب. Both are the same word; never mix them in one mouth. It replaces the formal ليس entirely.
vocabulary.image_scene: A red cross drawn over a picture of a house, a hand pointing to a different house.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone correcting a mistake — مو هذا، ذاك — with the objects on screen.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The verb negator, said as a short ma glued to the verb: ma-ashrab. It also negates the 'have' words (ما عندي، ما فيه). One word for every tense, so learn it once.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand held up flat in refusal in front of a glass of tea being offered.

example.english: I don't drink tea at night

vocabulary.video_hint: A refusal or a denial with ما + verb — ما أبي، ما أعرف، ما رحت.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Sits at the end of a ما sentence to make it absolute: ما أروح أبد. Also a one-word answer — أبد! 'not at all!'. Written أبداً in careful spelling. Kuwaitis also say كلش for 'at all'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A calendar with every square crossed out in red.

example.english: I never go to the market

vocabulary.video_hint: An emphatic denial — أبد! — in a sketch, often with a hand chop.

vocabulary.teaching_note: ما + أحد squeezed into one word with a doubled ḥ. It carries its own 'not', so the verb after it takes no ما: محد جا 'nobody came'. Spelled ما حد or محد online.
vocabulary.image_scene: An empty majlis with cushions along the walls and nobody in it.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone arriving to an empty place and saying محد هني / محد جا.

vocabulary.teaching_note: ولا 'not even' + شي 'thing'. Stronger than ما شي; it usually closes a ما sentence: ما أكلت ولا شي. Gulf شي has no hamza — the formal شيء is never said. Also the answer to شصار؟ — ولا شي 'nothing'.
vocabulary.image_scene: An empty plate and an empty glass on a table, a person shrugging.

example.english: I haven't eaten anything at all today

vocabulary.video_hint: The reply ولا شي to a question, or an exaggerated 'I've had nothing all day'.

vocabulary.teaching_note: للحين 'until now' + ما. Pan-Gulf; Jeddah says لسا ما. Alone, للحين answers 'married?' with 'not yet'. Do not confuse with الحين 'now' — the extra لـ makes it 'still'.
vocabulary.image_scene: An hourglass half-run, a person waiting beside an unopened lunchbox.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone explaining a task isn't done — للحين ما خلصت — in a vlog.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The busiest little word in the dialect. Here it means 'only': أبي بس ماي 'I just want water'. Said sharply on its own it means 'enough!' or 'stop'. It also does duty as the casual 'but' — you will hear it far more than لكن.
vocabulary.image_scene: A single glass of water alone on a large empty tray.
vocabulary.video_hint: بس with a raised palm to stop a pour, or بس واحد when ordering one item.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The clear 'but', used when the contrast matters: nice but expensive. In quick talk most Gulf speakers use بس for the same job, so hear لكن as the emphasised version. Long aa in the first syllable.
vocabulary.image_scene: A beautiful watch in a shop window with a very large price tag beside it.

example.english: The food is nice but expensive

vocabulary.video_hint: A review or complaint — حلو بس غالي / لكن — with the contrast visible.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Closes a topic: 'OK, done, no more'. خلاص شبعت ends the food negotiation; خلاص فهمت 'OK, got it'. Emphatic ص at the end. Universal across the Arab world, so a free win.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person pushing a finished plate away with both palms up, smiling.
vocabulary.video_hint: خلاص closing an argument or a meal in a sketch or family vlog.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Same as formal Arabic but very much alive in speech, usually as a shocked one-word reaction. For 'that's not on / can't be done' Gulf speakers prefer ما يصير, taught below.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person with both hands up and mouth open in disbelief in front of a giant bill.
vocabulary.video_hint: A shocked مستحيل! reaction to a price, a score or a piece of news.

vocabulary.teaching_note: ما + أبي, the Stage 1 'I want'. Riyadh says ما أبغى, the UAE ما أبا; all three are the same verb with a different amount of غ. Follow it with a noun (ما أبي قهوة) or a verb (ما أبي أروح). Never ما أريد.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand gently covering the top of a coffee cup as the pot approaches.
vocabulary.video_hint: Declining an offer — ما أبي / ما أبغى — at a table or in a shop.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'it doesn't concern'. Turned to the listener it becomes ولا يهمك 'don't worry about it', the standard reply to an apology. عادي 'normal, no big deal' does a similar job.
vocabulary.image_scene: A shrug with a relaxed smile, a spilled cup of tea on the table in front.

example.english: It doesn't matter, no big deal

vocabulary.video_hint: A reassurance after a small mishap — ما يهم / ولا يهمك — in a vlog.

vocabulary.english: that's not on / it can't be done
vocabulary.teaching_note: صار means 'to become / happen'; ما يصير is 'it doesn't happen' — the Gulf way to say something is not acceptable or not possible. Said with a shake of the head. The question يصير؟ asks 'is that OK?'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A shopkeeper shaking his head at a customer holding out too little money.
vocabulary.video_hint: A refusal of a request — ما يصير — in a customer-service sketch.

vocabulary.teaching_note: ما + عاد 'returned' = 'it no longer'. Put a present verb after it: ما عاد أشرب قهوة. Very Gulf; a learner who uses it sounds settled in the dialect.
vocabulary.image_scene: A coffee cup with a line through it and a glass of water beside it.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone describing a change of habit — ما عاد أروح / ما عاد آكل.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'Not like this?' — the tag that asks for agreement. كذا is Saudi and Qatari; Kuwaitis say مو جذي, Emiratis مب جي. The Egyptian كده is never used in the Gulf.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two friends looking at a sunset, one turning to the other with raised eyebrows.

example.english: The weather's nice today, isn't it?

vocabulary.video_hint: A speaker seeking agreement at the end of a sentence — مو كذا؟ / مو جذي؟

vocabulary.teaching_note: لا + والله 'by God'. This is the refusal that means it — the oath tells the host you are not just being polite. Also used for surprise: لا والله؟ 'no, really?'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A guest with a hand on their heart politely refusing a plate held out to them.

example.english: No, really, I don't want any

vocabulary.video_hint: A real refusal at a table — لا والله — with the host finally relenting.

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.arabic: ما أشرب قهوة بالليل، لكن شاي زين
dialogue.transliteration: ma ashrab gahwa bil-layl, laakin shaay zayn
dialogue.english: I don't drink coffee at night, but tea is fine

dialogue.speaker: Umm Fahad
dialogue.english: No problem, the tea is ready

sound_spotlight.explanation: The ma and the a- of the verb merge into one long maa: ma-ashrab sounds like maashrab. In captions you will still see two words; in your ear it is one.
ما + أحد collapses and the ḥ doubles: maḥ-ḥad. Hold the throat sound twice as long as you think you should.

sound_spotlight.sound: مو / مب — same word, different city
sound_spotlight.example: مو زين (mu zayn) / مب زين (mub zayn)
sound_spotlight.explanation: Kuwait and Saudi end it in a vowel, the UAE and Qatar in a b. You will hear both within one week of Gulf video; treat them as one word.

lesson_sequence.detail: A 45-second comedy clip of someone refusing, arguing and saying مستحيل — watched twice, the second time with the negation words highlighted in the captions.
Sixteen cards with illustration and audio. Each negation word plays inside a short sentence so the position (before verb, before noun, at the end) is heard, not read.
Grammar card: ما / مو / لا with one example each; then a sort — twenty sentence fragments dragged into the right box, with the verb or noun underlined as the clue.
Hear a positive sentence, tap the correct negated version from three options; the wrong options use the wrong particle.
Role-play: the app plays the insisting host three times; the learner refuses each time, escalating from لا شكراً to الله يخليك to والله شبعت.
Score screen with missed particles replayed. Nudge: notice today which 'no' you would need — a verb no, a noun no, or a command no.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Next time someone offers you food or coffee, refuse once politely — لا، الله يخليك — and see if they insist. Then accept.
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on the lesson-complete screen. Activates the ritual with a real host; the point is to feel the rhythm, not to refuse for real.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Say three true sentences about yourself with ما, مو and أبد: what you don't do, what you are not, and what you never do.
real_world_prompts.context: Speaking nudge the following day. Forces the ما / مو choice on the learner's own content.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Watch a Gulf sketch and count the مو or مب. Which one does the channel use? That is its city.
real_world_prompts.context: Homework card. Trains hearing the variant table as a signal about the speaker.

video_needs.scene: Someone declining, arguing or saying no way — a guest refusing food, a customer refusing a price, a character insisting ما يصير; comedy skits are full of it.
